Clever gradient-level averaging technique that avoids signal dilution in sparse reward settings
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 50 Metaworld tasks with detailed ablation studies

Major experimental fairness concern: T-SAC uses 5000 buffer size vs. SAC's 1e6 (200× difference), making sample efficiency comparisons unreliable
Inconsistent hyperparameter tuning across baselines: vastly different learning rates, batch sizes, and architectures suggest unequal tuning effort

Ablation studies insufficient: missing direct Transformer vs. MLP comparison, no sensitivity analysis for N, no gradient vs. target averaging comparison

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 50 Metaworld tasks plus Box-Pushing benchmarks provides broad scope
Clear problem motivation identifying genuine challenges in Q-function estimation, variance in N-step returns, and step-based control limitations
Mathematically correct variance analysis for averaged N-step returns (Section 2.3, Appendix B) provides theoretical grounding
Well-organized presentation with clear methodology descriptions and extensive hyperparameter details in appendices
Includes ablation studies attempting to isolate component contributions across multiple task subsets
weaknesses: Severely limited novelty: (1) Transformer critic directly adapts TOP-ERL with only step-based vs episodic policy difference; (2) N-step gradient averaging is straightforward engineering without rigorous justification; (3) action chunking at critic is design choice, not algorithmic contribution. Reads as combining existing techniques without sufficient innovation

Theoretical analysis is incomplete and flawed: variance formula (Eq. 4) assumes γ=1 and i.i.d. rewards (violated in practice), ignores bootstrap term variance (typically dominant in deep RL), and provides no formal proof that gradient-level averaging preserves variance reduction benefits

Unfair experimental comparisons: different hyperparameters across methods (learning rates, batch sizes, critic epochs, optimizers), different Update-to-Data ratios, different network architectures—no disclosure of hyperparameter tuning methodology. Raises fundamental fairness concerns

Suspicious baseline performance: SAC achieves 0% on Box-Pushing Sparse and 18% on Dense (unusually poor); CrossQ gets 0% Sparse—suggests potential implementation issues or inadequate baseline tuning, making T-SAC improvements questionable

Missing statistical rigor: Table 1 reports only aggregate success rates with no confidence intervals, error bars, or error statistics. Claims like '16% higher than second-best' cannot be assessed for significance without error bars. No statistical testing provided

Weak ablation studies: only 5-11 tasks (not all 50), covariance augmentation shows minimal IQM impact, entropy removal shows fragile mixed results (7/8 vs 5/8 runs, no statistical test). Suggests design choices are not robust

Architectural design choices lack principled justification: (1) feeding mean to covariance network—why? minimal ablation impact; (2) layer normalization—standard practice, not a contribution; (3) causal masking for critic—unexplained why future actions should affect Q-values causally

Incomplete comparisons: no direct empirical comparison to TOP-ERL despite using nearly identical architecture; missing comparisons to other Transformer-based RL methods, other multi-step approaches, and properly-tuned SAC baselines; SOTA claims unjustified without statistical testing

Theoretical justification for gradient-level averaging is circular: Section 3.1 claims it addresses 'signal dilution' in sparse rewards, but this is unproven. Why should gradient averaging of diverse targets G⁽¹⁾...G⁽ⁿ⁾ be better than return averaging? Not formally justified

Reproducibility concerns: no statement of code availability, enormous hyperparameter space with undisclosed tuning procedure, different initialization schemes across methods, missing computational cost analysis, no training time comparison, unclear number of random seeds per experiment

strengths: Strong empirical results: 16% improvement over SAC on MetaWorld (86% vs 70%) and exceptional sparse reward performance (58% vs ~0%)
Solid theoretical analysis of variance reduction in N-step returns with rigorous mathematical derivation (O(N) to O(N/3))
Practical gradient-level averaging strategy that avoids signal dilution in sparse reward environments
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 50 MetaWorld tasks and challenging dense/sparse Box-Pushing benchmarks
Clear presentation with detailed hyperparameters, ablation studies, and per-task results
Well-motivated use of Transformers to avoid gradient vanishing issues of RNNs in sequential processing
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing ideas (TOP-ERL + step-based policy + N-step returns); relationship to TOP-ERL insufficiently differentiated

Unfair experimental comparison: different data storage (trajectories vs transitions), unequal hyperparameter tuning depth, suspicious baseline performance (e.g., CrossQ at 0% on box-pushing), no computational cost analysis

Missing critical ablations: no MLP-based critic on sequence input to isolate Transformer contribution; no trajectory-storage SAC variant for fair comparison; ablations on limited task subsets (5-11 of 50 tasks)

Gradient-level averaging lacks mathematical rigor: claim that averaging ∇ϕLi provides equivalent variance reduction is assumed not proven; unclear how this recovers signal in sparse rewards where targets differ

Box-Pushing sparse results suspicious: all baselines achieve exactly 0% while T-SAC achieves 58%; insufficient statistical support (5-8 runs), no confidence intervals, possible task/reward-engineering bias
Design Choices 1 & 2 feel orthogonal: covariance augmentation has negligible IQM impact (Ablation 4.3.1); layer normalization is standard; these weaken main contribution claims

Reproducibility concerns: extensive per-algorithm tuning (varied learning rates, batch sizes, entropy coefficients), min/max_length selection criteria unexplained, code not mentioned, entropy ablation (4.3.3) shows improvement but not applied to final results
Missing statistical rigor: no significance tests, confidence intervals only in Figure 2, ablations use 5-8 runs without formal reporting of main experiment seeds
Insufficient recent baselines: comparisons mainly to 2017-2020 methods; missing recent off-policy approaches and no empirical comparison to closely related TOP-ERL despite citation
Misleading 'action chunking' framing: critic processes sequences but doesn't chunk in traditional sense; actor still outputs single actions; relationship to temporal abstraction unclear
Policy network contributions poorly isolated: entropy regularization study (4.3.3) contradicts SAC theory with speculative explanations; why remove entropy if beneficial?

strengths: Strong empirical results on Meta-World multi-phase tasks and Box-Pushing (96.8% success), demonstrating clear advantages for long-horizon manipulation
Clever technical innovation in gradient-level N-step return averaging that avoids importance sampling while preserving sparse reward signals, with rigorous theoretical justification (Appendices C-D)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 57 tasks with thorough ablations, consistent evaluation protocol (8 seeds, confidence intervals), and detailed hyperparameter specifications enabling reproducibility
Effective positioning that addresses a real gap between step-based methods (efficient but myopic) and episodic methods (better credit assignment but complex)
Solid theoretical analysis of variance reduction with detailed proofs and practical insights on value reuse and sparse-reward propagation
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (Transformer critics from TOP-ERL, standard N-step returns, causal masking); individual components are known

Inconsistent performance across domains: mixed results on MuJoCo locomotion (strong on some tasks, weak on others); requires action masking and task-specific configuration; modest gains vs. SAC/TD3/CrossQ on standard benchmarks

Weaker sparse-reward performance (58% on Box-Pushing sparse vs. 70% for TOP-ERL) with acknowledged instability requiring conventional target networks, contradicting the sparse-reward credit assignment motivation

Task-specific tuning undermines generality: different UTD ratios per benchmark, separate target-free vs. target-network schemes, action masks required for certain tasks; unclear hyperparameter sensitivity

Comparison fairness issues: T-SAC extensively tuned while many baselines taken from published papers; TOP-ERL comparison complicated by different paradigms (episodic vs. step-based); CrossQ on Box-Pushing capped at 10M steps

Limited justification for design choices: unclear why Transformers outperform simpler sequence models (GRU/LSTM ablation superficial), weak motivation for non-soft critic design, insufficient connection between theory and empirical gains
Target-free training limited to local-motion tasks and requires reversion to conventional networks for sparse rewards, limiting scope and generality of the approach

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 57 tasks with rigorous statistical reporting (IQM, bootstrap CIs)
Strong results on Meta-World ML1 manipulation tasks, solving most within 5M steps
Thorough theoretical analysis of N-step variance reduction with formal proofs in Appendix C
Extensive ablation studies examining Transformer components, step length, sampling density, and baseline comparisons
Clear positioning as a bridge between step-based (SAC) and episodic (TOP-ERL) methods with well-articulated motivation
Good reproducibility effort with detailed hyperparameters (Tables 1-4), algorithm pseudocode, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Transformer architecture directly adapted from TOP-ERL, N-step returns are standard, and importance-sampling avoidance mirrors prior work; contribution is primarily system design

Unfair experimental comparisons: baselines from prior publications with different seeds (PPO/gSDE: 20, T-SAC: 8) and different training budgets acknowledged but not resolved; evaluation protocol differs from TOP-ERL (per-task vs pooled IQM)

Significant domain-dependent limitations not adequately addressed: weak on Hopper/Walker2d locomotion tasks, requires action masks, necessitates task-specific entropy targets (H_target = -4×dim(A) for some tasks), and parameter-freezing strategy fails on sparse rewards

Sparse reward performance contradicts generality claims: achieves 58% on Box-Pushing sparse vs TOP-ERL's 70%, though paper claims 'competitive' performance; requires reverting to standard target networks

Shallow justification for key design choices: non-soft critic design lacks principled motivation beyond citing other methods; gradient-level vs target-level averaging justified indirectly through Fig. 10b rather than direct comparison; action masking relegated to appendix despite being critical

Incomplete analysis of core contributions: parameter-freezing schedule lacks theoretical insight; why hard refresh causes instability on sparse Box-Pushing (Fig. 10a) unexplained; gradient averaging benefits over alternatives not rigorously quantified

Experimental inconsistencies undermine ablation reliability: sparse Box-Pushing uses only 4 seeds 'due to compute limits'; some ablations use 16M steps (step length) or 10M steps (GRU/LSTM) vs standard 20M; makes interpretation unreliable

Computational overhead underexamined: T-SAC takes 3.09 hours vs SAC's 1.47 hours for 1M steps (Fig. 2), but cost-benefit analysis absent; multiple Transformer passes and 4 supervision windows per step add complexity

Missing critical comparisons: no comparison to other recent Transformer-based RL methods, variance-reduction techniques (Retrace, QpropRetrace), or ablation isolating entropy-regularization design choice

Presentation issues: 34-page paper with critical limitations scattered across appendices (action masks, instability, domain-specific fixes); misleading framing as 'state-of-the-art' without noting evaluation protocol differences from TOP-ERL; limited discussion of why method excels on manipulation but struggles on locomotion

strengths: Strong empirical results on Meta-World ML1 (50 tasks) with state-of-the-art aggregated IQM, solving most tasks in ~5M steps; comprehensive evaluation across 57 diverse tasks with proper statistical methodology (IQM, 95% CI, multiple seeds)
Elegant technical approach: avoids importance sampling complexity by predicting prefix-conditioned values for realized action sequences from replay, enabling stable N-step learning up to n=16

Solid theoretical contributions: Appendix C provides rigorous variance analysis showing N-step averaging reduces target variance by factor 1-4 under equicorrelated assumptions; Appendix D analyzes gradient-level averaging in shared-weight Transformers

Practical simplicity: lightweight architecture (2-layer Transformer, 128-256 units), low computational overhead, works at low UTD ratios, no need for complex mechanisms like batch normalization or constrained activations

Thorough experimental rigor: comprehensive ablation studies (Transformer components, window lengths, architectures), detailed hyperparameter documentation, algorithm flowcharts, and reproducibility efforts in appendix
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: contribution is primarily careful engineering combining existing techniques (Transformer critics from TOP-ERL, N-step returns, gradient averaging, parameter freezing from CrossQ) rather than introducing fundamental innovations

Mixed performance across domains: weak results on locomotion tasks (Hopper, Walker2d), sparse-reward gap (58% vs TOP-ERL's 70% on Box-Pushing Sparse), requires different UTD ratios per domain (1 vs 0.75 vs 0.25) and task-specific entropy tuning

Unfair baseline comparisons: Meta-World results mix tuned baselines (SAC, CrossQ) with untuned baselines from prior publications; different evaluation protocol than TOP-ERL (per-task vs pooled IQM); some baselines given larger budgets

Incomplete understanding of failure modes: paper acknowledges performance issues on sparse rewards and high-variance locomotion but lacks principled explanation; App. G provides post-hoc analysis rather than design-time insights; no characterization of when to use T-SAC

Theoretical gaps: variance analysis assumes restrictive equicorrelated structure; no convergence guarantees; parameter freezing motivation (§4.4) is informal despite claims about theoretical justification; gap between proven variance reduction and claimed training stability
